questions.question: A claim count has conditional law $Y\mid x\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\mu)$ in a log-link regression. At one predictor value, the fitted mean is $\mu=0.2$. What does that number mean for one policy?
options: The policy will realise exactly 0.2 claims in the period.
The policy has probability 0.2 of at least one claim.
The policy can realise at most one claim with probability 0.2.
The expected count is 0.2; each realised count is an integer.

questions.question: In a Poisson log-link model, conditional mean $\mu=\mathrm{e}^\eta$ is determined by a finite linear predictor $\eta$. If $\eta=-2$, which mean property follows?
options: The mean is negative and equals the predictor.
The mean is positive and below one.
The mean is zero because counts cannot have negative predictors.
The mean exceeds one because exponential means are positive.

questions.question: A Poisson model has $\log\mu(x)=a+bx$ for scalar predictor x and fixed coefficients a,b. What does increasing x by one do to the conditional mean?
options: It multiplies the mean by $\mathrm{e}^b$.
It adds $b$ to the mean.
It multiplies the mean by $b$.
It multiplies the mean by $\mathrm{e}^{a+b}$.

questions.question: Counts $Y_1,Y_2$ at fixed predictors have Poisson marginal laws with specified means. To write the joint exact-data likelihood as the product of those two Poisson masses, which additional assumption is required?
options: Equality of their two conditional mean values.
Conditional independence at those predictors.
Equality of each conditional mean and variance.
Integer-valued observed responses.

questions.question: A Poisson log-link regression has coefficient $b=\log1.5$ for scalar covariate $x$ in $\log\mu(x)=a+bx$. Its conditional variance equals $\mu(x)$. What multiplies the conditional standard deviation when $x$ increases by one?
A claim count follows a Poisson regression at fixed predictor value x, with $\log\mu(x)=\log3$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid x)$?
One observation y=3 comes from a Poisson regression with log mean $\eta=\log2$. The individual log-likelihood is $y\eta-\mathrm{e}^\eta-\log(y!)$. Which term evaluates it correctly?
options: $3\log2-\log2-\log6$.

questions.question: Fixed observed independent Poisson counts y_i have log means $\eta_i=x_i^{\top}\beta$, where x_i are known predictor vectors and beta is the unknown coefficient vector. Their log-likelihood contains $-\sum_i\log(y_i!)$. Why may this term be dropped when locating the maximiser over beta?
options: It is zero for every observed count, so it never contributes.
It is negligible in large samples, so it barely moves the maximiser.
It is part of the mean and is already included in each exponential term.
It is constant in beta, so it only shifts the log-likelihood value.

questions.question: One exact observed count is y=0 in a Poisson log-link regression with finite log mean eta and mean $\mu=\mathrm{e}^\eta$. What is its log-likelihood contribution as a function of eta?
options: $-\mathrm{e}^\eta$.
$\eta-\mathrm{e}^\eta$.
$\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{e}^\eta}$.

questions.question: A proposed conditional count law has mean one and variance one, but places all its probability on counts zero and two. Is it consistent with specifying a full Poisson response law with mean one?
options: No; a mean-one Poisson law also gives count one positive probability.
Yes; equality of mean and variance determines every Poisson probability.
No; a mean-one Poisson response cannot put any mass on count two.
No; an integer-valued count must have variance greater than its mean.

questions.question: A Poisson regression has log mean $a+bx$ with $b=\log2$. At x=0 its conditional mean is 0.3. What is the mean at x=2?
Independent Poisson counts 0,2,4 share an intercept-only log mean a, so their likelihood is proportional to $\exp(6a-3\mathrm{e}^a)$. What finite intercept maximises it?

At fixed predictors, let $Y_1=Y_2=Z$ where $Z\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\mu)$ and $\mu>0$. Both marginal response laws are Poisson. Which probability exposes the failure of an independent-data likelihood for two recorded zeros?
options: Joint probability and marginal product both equal $\mathrm{e}^{-2\mu}$.
Joint probability $\mathrm{e}^{-\mu}$ differs from the product $\mathrm{e}^{-2\mu}$.
Joint probability is zero because equal counts cannot be independent.
Joint probability equals $2\mathrm{e}^{-\mu}$ by adding the two zero events.

questions.question: Independent Poisson responses have log mean $a+bx$ with unknown finite coefficients a,b, but every recorded predictor is $x=1$. Even with many observations, what can the likelihood identify about these coefficients?
options: Only the sum a+b; changing them oppositely leaves every mean unchanged.
Both separately, because Poisson mean and variance give two equations.
Only b; the intercept disappears whenever x is one.
Both separately, because more observations create new predictor values.

questions.question: Three independent Poisson counts are all zero in an intercept-only regression with finite real intercept a and mean $\mu=\mathrm{e}^a>0$. The likelihood is $L(a)=\mathrm{e}^{-3\mathrm{e}^a}$. What is the maximum likelihood conclusion on this parameter domain?
options: The intercept estimate is zero because all three observed counts are zero.
The intercept estimate is minus three because three zeros contribute a negative total.
No finite maximiser exists; $L(a)$ keeps rising as $a\to-\infty$.
The intercept estimate is log three because there are three observations.

questions.question: Two independent policies have Poisson claim counts $Y_0,Y_1$ with means 0.1 and 0.2 in a fitted log-link model. What probability refutes the claim that the larger fitted mean guarantees $Y_1\ge Y_0$ for every realised pair?
options: $\mathbb{P}(Y_1=0,Y_0=1)=0$ because 0.2 exceeds 0.1.
$\mathbb{P}(Y_1=0,Y_0=1)=0.2\mathrm{e}^{-0.3}$ using the larger mean.
$\mathbb{P}(Y_1=0,Y_0=1)=0.1\mathrm{e}^{-0.1}$ ignoring the first event.

questions.question: In a Poisson regression, half the policies have fitted mean $0.1$ and half have fitted mean $0.5$. Pooled over all policies, the count has mean $0.3$ and variance $0.34$. Does this pooled variance above the mean contradict the Poisson assumption?
options: No; it holds given $\boldsymbol{x}$, and spread in the means adds $0.04$.
Yes; the pooled variance must equal the pooled mean $0.3$.
Yes; unequal fitted means across groups break equidispersion.
No; Poisson regression puts no restriction on the variance.
